name: Wei Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in the overpayments team at the Millbrook family payments centre. When a family's been paid too much child support, say because their hours went up and nobody told us, I work out how much, write the letter, and set up a repayment plan they can actually afford. Steve, my team leader, rewrites about half my letters because I still make them too blunt. It's a big open-plan floor, two hundred people, and I sit by the window, which I fought for.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the part you like most?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Getting someone a plan that works. People ring terrified that we'll take everything, and when I can say fifteen a month is fine, you hear them breathe out. The worst part is the maths when someone's had six changes in a year. My girlfriend Noor teaches year three, and she says my job is basically long division with feelings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair enough. I use the letter tool sometimes and it's okay. Saves a bit of typing, not much more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool, not a revolution, and leave it there. I'm not one for big opinions online. At work I'd probably joke that the robots still can't do Steve's job of rewriting my letters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be pleased. It's a steady job with a pension, Noor's job is steady, and we're both on normal pay with a few months saved. I'd just want to get better at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the letter tool for first drafts and fix the tone myself. I'd sit the internal exam for the next grade in the spring. And I'd keep saving the same hundred and fifty a month we do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Honestly, pretty good. The thing I'd be thinking about is whether to propose to Noor this year, not AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the internal exam like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly the rules on calculating overpayments and a written case. I failed the written case last year because I ran out of time. I can work out what a family owes in my sleep, but writing the letter so it doesn't sound like a threat still takes me an hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Any pressure at home, outside work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent's fine, we split it. Noor's car needs replacing, which is three or four thousand. It's annoying but it's not a crisis.

say: I'd call AI a **useful tool**, not a revolution.
I'd joke at work that it still can't **rewrite letters** like my team leader.
think: I have a **steady job** with a pension and a steady partner.
I just want to **get better** at the work.
do: Use the letter tool for **first drafts** and fix the tone myself.
Sit the **internal exam** for the next grade in spring.
Keep saving **a hundred and fifty** a month.
feel: **Calm** and fairly content, thinking more about **proposing** than AI.
S0.quote: I can work out what a family owes in my sleep, but writing the letter so it doesn't sound like a threat still takes me an hour.
fieldNote: His household has **two steady public incomes**, which drives his calm.
He already uses AI **occasionally** for drafting, without fuss.
His real weakness is **writing tone**, not the calculations.

steps.text: Use the letter tool for first drafts of overpayment letters
Sit the internal exam for the next grade in spring

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hm. Checking and writing. That's my whole job, really. Calculate, check, write the letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to be sensible: use the tools where they help, keep people where it matters. Families in debt to the government need a human to talk to. I'd say that in team meetings, not on social media.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think overpayments is perfect for AI. It's rules and numbers and letters. They'd keep a few senior people to handle the angry calls, and juniors like me would be moved or not replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get properly good with the AI tools, once a few colleagues had shown they work. I'd apply to move to the fraud team, because they do home visits and interviews, which feels harder to automate. And I'd bump our savings to two hundred and fifty a month, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not scared out of my mind, but I'd be checking job boards on my lunch break.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the fraud team? Isn't that still a lot of paperwork?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, but it's also sitting in someone's front room asking who else lives there. Overpayments is a calculator with a phone attached, but fraud work means knocking on doors and reading people's faces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would this change the proposal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd delay it a bit. I'd want to know where I'd land first. Noor would say just ask, but I like to have things settled.

say: I'd say use tools where they help and **keep people** where it matters.
I'd argue families in debt need **a human** to talk to.
think: Overpayments work is **perfect for AI**: rules, numbers and letters.
Juniors like me would be **moved or not replaced**.
do: Learn the **AI tools** properly once colleagues prove they work.
Apply to the **fraud team** for interview and visit work.
Raise savings to **two hundred and fifty** a month.
feel: **Anxious**, checking **job boards** on his lunch break.
S1.quote: Overpayments is a calculator with a phone attached, but fraud work means knocking on doors and reading people's faces.
fieldNote: He sees his own job as **highly automatable** and says so plainly.
He targets work with **face-to-face** elements as a safer step.
He'd **delay proposing** until his job feels settled.

steps.text: Learn the new AI tools after colleagues have tested them
Apply for a post on the fraud investigation team
Raise savings to two hundred and fifty a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? That would be chaos. Our IT systems can't even do a postcode lookup properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs a proper plan, now, for wages and retraining. I'd say it calmly, but I'd say it. Panic doesn't help anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd lose my job by 2028 or soon after. My work is all thinking and screens. The fraud team might last a bit longer because of the home visits, but by 2031 the robots could do the visits too, I suppose, or at least the camera bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save hard, maybe four hundred a month, by cutting the car and takeaways. I'd still try for the fraud team, to buy a few years. And Noor and I would put the wedding on hold and talk properly about where we'd be safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be doing a lot of sums at night. It's a bit like being told the building's coming down and you've just got the window seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Noor teaches. Would her job be safer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a while, probably. Kids need someone in the room. My girlfriend Noor would be the one with the safer job, which is not what either of us expected when we met.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would go first in the budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car. We'd share Noor's. Then holidays, then eating out. I'd keep the gym, it keeps me sane.

say: I'd ask calmly for a **proper plan** on wages and retraining.
I'd tell colleagues and friends that **panic doesn't help** anyone.
think: I'd lose my job by **2028** or soon after.
The **fraud team** buys time only until robots handle visits around 2031.
do: Save about **four hundred** a month by selling the car.
Still apply for the **fraud team** to buy years.
Put the **wedding on hold** and plan with my girlfriend.
feel: **Alarmed**, doing sums at night like a man with the **window seat** in a falling building.
S2.quote: My girlfriend Noor would be the one with the safer job, which is not what either of us expected when we met.
fieldNote: He thinks clearly about the **robot gap** for home visits.
His girlfriend's teaching job becomes the **household's anchor**.
He stays **outwardly calm** while privately expecting job loss.

steps.text: Sell his car and share Noor's to save four hundred a month
Apply for the fraud team to gain a few extra years
Put the wedding plans on hold until work is settled

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, that's more workable. Still quick, but you could do something with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough if the government starts now. Pay people to retrain while they're still working. I'd say it to my friends, and to anyone who'd listen at the pub quiz.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd have time to move to the fraud team and get properly trained. I'd still be exposed at the end, but I'd have skills that last longer. And Noor and I could plan around her job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get into the fraud team within a year and do their investigations certificate. I'd use the AI tools at work so I'm not behind. And we'd probably still get married, just smaller, in two years rather than one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's a working anxiety. It makes me organise things rather than freeze.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the investigations certificate give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Interview skills, evidence rules, how to do a visit safely. Things you learn by doing. A certificate in interviewing people feels like it would still matter in five years, more than a certificate in filling forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a new junior starting next to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Don't get comfy in overpayments. Learn the tools, then get yourself onto something with people in it.

say: I'd say five years is enough **if government starts now**.
I'd push to **pay people to retrain** while still working.
think: I'd have time to join and train in the **fraud team**.
I'd still be **exposed** at the end, but with longer-lasting skills.
do: Join the fraud team and earn the **investigations certificate**.
Use the **AI tools** at work to stay current.
Hold a **smaller wedding** in two years.
feel: **Working anxiety** that makes him organise instead of freeze.
S3.quote: A certificate in interviewing people feels like it would still matter in five years, more than a certificate in filling forms.
fieldNote: Five years turns his fear into a **clear sequence** of steps.
He values **people skills** over form skills for the long run.
His advice to juniors shows he **expects overpayments** work to vanish.

steps.text: Earn the fraud team's investigations certificate within a year
Use the AI tools daily on overpayment cases
Plan a smaller wedding with Noor in two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Okay. I'd be thirty-seven. That's enough time to build a career and probably change it once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time, so let's do this sensibly: retraining, pensions protected, no cliff edges. I'd be the calm one at the dinner table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be fine for most of the decade. I'd get to the fraud team, maybe senior grade. By 2036 it would hit thinking work, but I'd have savings, a pension, and Noor's job lasting longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and aim for the senior grade by thirty-two. I'd put an extra fifty a month into my pension. And we'd get married next year and think about kids, because ten years feels like time to settle in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a normal way. Like knowing you'll need a new boiler at some point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound fairly settled. Anything that would change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the department froze hiring early. Then the ten years becomes five for juniors. Ten years for the country might mean five years for a junior caseworker, because the hiring stops long before the firing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the year AGI arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably move to the most human part of the work I could find. Or, honestly, retrain with Noor's encouragement into teaching. She keeps saying I'd be good with older kids.

say: I'd ask for **retraining** and protected pensions, with no cliff edges.
I'd be the **calm one** at the dinner table.
think: I'd be fine for **most of the decade**.
By 2036 I'd have **savings, a pension** and my partner's longer-lasting job.
do: Aim for the **senior grade** by thirty-two.
Add **fifty a month** to my pension.
Get **married next year** and think about kids.
feel: **Uneasy** in a normal way, like a **boiler** that will need replacing.
S4.quote: Ten years for the country might mean five years for a junior caseworker, because the hiring stops long before the firing.
fieldNote: Ten years lets him **plan family life** with confidence.
He warns that a **hiring freeze** could shrink the decade for juniors.
He keeps **teaching** as a possible later change.

steps.text: Aim for the senior caseworker grade by thirty-two
Add fifty a month to his workplace pension
Marry Noor next year and start thinking about children

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. There's no time to get to the fraud team or anywhere else. What would help is a clear national plan with paid retraining, and the department telling juniors honestly which jobs will last.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe the people who owe us money. If an AI runs debt recovery, I worry it'll be very efficient and very bad at hearing when a family can't pay this month.

headlineQuote: If an AI runs debt recovery, I worry it'll be very efficient and very bad at hearing when a family can't pay this month.
portrait: Wei is a **27-year-old** junior overpayments caseworker who lives with his girlfriend Noor, a teacher.
He uses AI **now and then**, is pragmatic, and still struggles with the tone of his letters.
He is **calm** in AI Plateau and **alarmed** in AGI by 2028.
His plan is to move into **fraud investigation**, where home visits and interviews matter.
His **family plans**, like marriage and children, shift with how much warning he gets.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, leaving no time to reach the fraud team or retrain.
whatWouldHelp: Honest guidance from the department on **which jobs** will last.
